newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia government seen unveiling mild budget.
newsitem.headline: Australia government seen unveiling mild budget.

text.p: Australia's conservative government was due on Tuesday to unveil a mild budget aimed at winding back the deficit and creating jobs.
Treasurer Peter Costello said the budget for the fiscal year from July would cement the economic gains of the Liberal-National coalition's first 14 months in power.
"This will be a responsible budget and it will confirm the economic progress we've made over the last year," Costello told reporters as he arrived at parliament house.
"It will also be directed towards our priorities for the coming year in relation to jobs and families and small business."

Economists said on Tuesday they expected budget cuts of A$1.0 billion (US$780 million) to A$1.5 billion to produce an underlying deficit -- which excludes windfalls such as asset sales -- of around A$2.5 billion.
The government has projected an A$8.5 billion underlying deficit for the year to June 30, 1997.

Australian markets were restrained in early trading on Tuesday, but optimistic the official budget announcement at 7.30 p.m. (0930 GMT) would cement the fiscal improvement set in place in the 1996/97 budget, traders said.
The winners in this budget were likely to be business, middle and rural Australia and defence.

Costello was expected to announce extensive tax rebates to encourage low and middle income earners to save more, continue business aid schemes to encourage job creation and offer cash bonuses to older workers to keep working and not claim pensions.
Costello was expected to cut back on health and public housing, reduce benefits including childcare assitance for higher income earners, and reduce subsidies for medicines.
Canberra measures its economic performance against the underlying budget, which removes windfall items such as asset sales and debt repayments by state and territory governments.
But asset sales, including the one-third privatisation of telecoms giant Telstra Corp, are expected to push the bottom line to about a A$10 billion surplus.
Last year's budget, the first by a conservative administration in 14 years, slashed spending by A$7 billion and sparked sometimes violent demonstrations around the country.
